raw_case_text:
A 6 year old boy who was born and lived in Cameroon for four years, in a rural area, was admitted to the Emergency Department with seizure lasting more than thirty minutes, not responsive to Diazepam 0.5 mg/Kg e.r. The patient had immigrated to Italy two years previously. No familiarity for seizures or headache. At the age of 1 year the child had experienced an acute and isolated febrile seizure with oculogyration. He had no recent history of traumatic or infective episodes, neither ingestion of drugs or weight loss. When he woke up that morning, he had speaking difficulties, right deviation of the mouth, followed by right head and gaze deviation, right emiclonic convulsion, and loss of consciousness. At admission the child was afebrile, unconscious, with accelerated heart rate and respiratory difficulties. His head was deviated to the right, there was a generalized hypertonia with hyperextension of right arm and flexion of the left arm. The electroencephalogram (EEG) detected a slow mono-polymorphic activity on the left and central electroencephalographic leads. This activity was absent on the right leads. It suggested a post-critical focal cerebral suffering.
He was directly admitted to the Intensive Care Unit and he was successfully treated with Phenobarbital (5 mg/Kg i.v.). The magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed two cystic round lesions located one in the right lentiform nucleus and one in the left frontal-parietal lobe (Figure 1). In the following 36 hours the EEG displayed an improvement of child's cerebral conditions with the disappearance of the asymmetric slow activity reported previously. After 48 hours the child was transferred to our Department. Blood exams revealed high eosinophil cell count (720 cells/muL) and Ig E levels (217 UI/ml). Western blot assay detected specific antibodies against cysticercus (LDBIO DIAGNOSTICS, Lyon, France). Therefore the diagnosis of neurocysticercosis was made and the appropriated therapy was started: the child received, orally, albendazole (15 mg/Kg/day) in two divided doses and dexamethasone (2 mg/day) for eight days.
Six months later, the eosinophil and IgE levels got back to normal. At brain MRI calcified areas, corresponding to the previous lesions, were indicated, without any new active lesions (Figure 2).
In the following two years the patient remained seizure-free on oral antiepileptic therapy. Then the patient has been lost to follow up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 6-year-old Cameroonian boy presented to the emergency department in focal-to-bilateral status epilepticus lasting over 30 minutes.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Upon awakening on the morning of admission, the child developed difficulty speaking and rightward mouth deviation, rapidly followed by right head and gaze deviation, right hemiclonic convulsions, and loss of consciousness lasting more than 30 minutes and unresponsive to rectal diazepam (0.5 mg/kg).
subjective.past_medical_history: Born and lived in a rural area of Cameroon for his first 4 years before immigrating to Italy 2 years prior to presentation. At 1 year of age, he experienced a single isolated febrile seizure with oculogyration. Family history was negative for seizures or headache, and there was no recent trauma, infection, drug ingestion, or weight loss.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for recent fever, trauma, drug ingestion, or weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, he was afebrile and unconscious with tachycardia, respiratory distress, rightward head deviation, and generalized hypertonia characterized by right arm hyperextension and left arm flexion.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood tests demonstrated peripheral eosinophilia (720 cells/mcL) and elevated serum IgE (217 IU/mL).
objective.advanced_workup: Admission electroencephalogram (EEG) showed slow mono-polymorphic postictal activity over the left and central leads (absent on the right), which resolved on repeat EEG 36 hours later. Brain MRI revealed two round parenchymal cystic lesions located in the right lentiform nucleus and the left frontoparietal lobe.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Serum Western blot assay (LDBIO Diagnostics) detected specific antibodies against Cysticercus, confirming parenchymal neurocysticercosis. Status epilepticus was controlled in the ICU with intravenous phenobarbital (5 mg/kg), followed by oral albendazole (15 mg/kg/day in two divided doses) and dexamethasone (2 mg/day) for 8 days. At 6-month follow-up, eosinophil count and IgE levels normalized and repeat brain MRI showed residual calcifications at the prior lesion sites without new active cysts. He remained seizure-free on oral antiepileptic therapy over 2 years of follow-up.
